title: Learning limit cycles via Hebbian synaptic plasticity
authors: Samantha J. Fournier, Luca Vincenzo Spallanzani, Pierfrancesco Urbani
abstract: We investigate high-dimensional, non-linear dynamical systems when exposed to incoherent periodic inputs and Hebbian-like synaptic plasticity. Our findings reveal a striking phenomenon: depending on the interplay between the strength of the periodic drive and synaptic plasticity, the system's phase diagram can give rise to a region where, once both inputs are removed, the collective dynamics spontaneously settles into a limit cycle. This suggests that periodic drives can imprint lasting rhythmic patterns into the network through plasticity, effectively teaching it to oscillate on its own. Numerical simulations on finite size systems show that the limit cycle phase can be easily detected on single-sample trajectories, while averaged curves are affected by strong finite size effects due to sample-to-sample fluctuations of the period of the limit cycles.
summary: This paper models high-dimensional neural networks subject to periodic external drives and Hebbian synaptic plasticity. It theoretically demonstrates that the network can 'learn' a stable, self-sustained rhythmic pattern—a limit cycle—even after the initial driving forces are removed. The findings highlight how plasticity allows transient inputs to imprint lasting oscillatory memories onto the system's connectivity.
main_problem: The study investigates whether limit cycle activity, transiently induced by external periodic stimulation in high-dimensional neural networks, can be stabilized through Hebbian synaptic plasticity.
main_result: The system exhibits a novel regime where the interplay of periodic drive and plasticity imprints a memory of rhythmic patterns onto network connectivity, causing the dynamics to spontaneously settle into a limit cycle after the external inputs are removed.
method: The analysis employs Dynamical Mean Field Theory (DMFT) in the thermodynamic limit ($N 	o \infty$) to characterize the system's phase diagram and time evolution.
model_or_system: The model is a high-dimensional, non-linear dynamical system incorporating Hebbian synaptic plasticity. The dynamics are governed by external periodic inputs and internal coupling terms that evolve based on past activity.
key_observables: Two-time correlation function $C(t, t')$, Mean Square Displacement (MSD) $Y(t, t')$, and the period of the resulting limit cycle ($T^*$).
important_parameters: Driving amplitude ($I$), plasticity coupling strength ($k$), and the metabolic phase duration ($\Delta_{me} = T_{ht} - T_{st}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on DMFT in the $N 	o \infty$ limit, and later sections involve approximating the dynamics by decomposing degrees of freedom into two uncorrelated stochastic processes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the phase diagram showing transitions between chaotic, fixed point, and limit cycle attractors based on parameters. Later figures show the lifetime of persistent oscillations ($T_{lt}$) versus input strength and the effect of $\Delta_{me}$ on attractor type.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the model dynamics under periodic drive and plasticity. It then analyzes the resulting phase diagram using DMFT to identify regimes supporting limit cycles. Finally, it investigates the robustness of these learned rhythms by varying the metabolic time window ($\Delta_{me}$).
why_interesting: This work provides a theoretical framework for how complex, sustained rhythmic behaviors (limit cycles) can emerge and persist in artificial neural networks purely through local learning rules (Hebbian plasticity), which has implications for understanding biological rhythm generation.

The lifetime Tlt is defined as the time interval over which C(t, Tst), plotted as a function of t −Tst, displays sustained oscillations. Numerically, Tlt is obtained by locating the point after the final oscillation peak where |∂tC(t, Tst)| falls below a fixed threshold. (Right) Impact of a non-zero metabolic phase ∆me = Tht −Tst on the limit cycle attractor of the memorization phase (t ≥t′ ≫Tht). As long as ∆me is sufficiently small compared to Tlt, the MSD vanishes periodically, indicating limit cycle activity (shades of viridis). Parameters are: I = 2, k = 3.5.
